source_title: How Prevalent Are Credit-Constrained Firms in the Formal Sector? Evidence from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys (Policy Research Working Paper 10502)
publisher_issuer: World Bank Group (Enterprise Surveys / Development Research Group)
company_context: Population-level firm dataset, not a single company. The World Bank Enterprise Surveys are nationally representative firm-level surveys of the private sector across 160+ economies, predominantly emerging and developing markets. This working paper analyzes a cross-section of over 65,000 formal-sector firms across 109 economies surveyed between 2013 and 2022, measuring how many firms are credit constrained.
business_type: Cross-sectoral formal private-sector firms (manufacturing, retail, services) in emerging and developing economies, skewed toward small and medium enterprises
company_size_stage: Mixed; predominantly small and medium enterprises in emerging markets, with large firms included for comparison
geography: 109 economies across Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Latin America, Middle East/North Africa, Europe/Central Asia, East Asia (non-US, emerging-market focus)
macro_context: Spans pre-pandemic and pandemic-era credit conditions across developing economies; structurally thin formal credit markets in lower-income economies.
outcome_category: 20 - ambiguous/insufficient evidence (population base-rate distribution, no firm-level outcome)
evidence_summary: Across 109 economies, about 30 percent of formal-sector firms are credit constrained. The paper classifies firms as fully credit constrained (no external financing and either did not apply due to expected obstacles or applied and were rejected), partially credit constrained (have external financing but are discouraged from applying for more, or were only partially approved), or unconstrained. Credit-constrained firms tend to be smaller and are geographically concentrated in Africa, and are less productive than unconstrained firms after controls. This establishes a population base rate for financing/working-capital constraints rather than a single-firm outcome, making it appropriate for abstention rather than a confident firm-level diagnosis.

source_backed_metrics.firms_credit_constrained_share: about 30 percent of firms across the 109-economy sample
source_backed_metrics.credit_constraint_categories: fully credit constrained (FCC), partially credit constrained (PCC), unconstrained (UC)

owner_decision_context: Not applicable at firm level; the dataset characterizes the prevalence of financing constraints faced by owners/managers across a population of emerging-market firms.
action_taken: Not applicable; this is a measurement study, not a single-firm intervention narrative.
outcome_evidence: No firm-level outcome is reported. The reported result is a population statistic: roughly 30 percent of firms are credit constrained, with constrained firms smaller, less productive, and concentrated in Africa.
source_limitations: Population dataset with no individual-firm outcome trajectory; cannot support a confident single-company diagnosis. Self-reported survey constructs (discouraged borrowers, perceived obstacles) introduce measurement subjectivity. Cross-section pooled across 2013-2022 waves, so it mixes time periods. PDF full text returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch; figures confirmed verbatim in World Bank/Enterprise Surveys primary-domain search snippets.
directly_stated: About 30 percent of firms across 109 economies are credit constrained
Sample covers over 65,000 firms across 109 economies, 2013-2022
Three categories: fully credit constrained, partially credit constrained, unconstrained
Credit-constrained firms tend to be smaller and are concentrated in Africa
Credit-constrained firms are less productive than unconstrained firms after controls
inferred: The ~30 percent base rate is a reasonable prior for working-capital/financing stress among emerging-market SMEs
Absence of firm-level outcome data means a confident single-firm diagnosis is not supportable from this source alone
why_useful_for_opsiq: Provides a credible non-US, emerging-market base rate for financing/working-capital constraints. Useful for teaching OpsIQ to abstain (outcome 20) when only population priors are available and no firm-specific evidence supports a confident diagnosis, and for calibrating the prevalence of working_capital_stress in the SME population.
